thread.title: 83-Year-Old Fred Fusaro Coaches Huntington Football After 55 Years on Long Island
thread.title_full: 83-Year-Old Fred Fusaro Coaches Huntington Football After 55 Years on Long Island

author: nypost
title: 83-Year-Old Fred Fusaro Coaches Huntington Football After 55 Years on Long Island
text:
Fred Fusaro, 83, coaches offensive line at Huntington High School after 55 years, four NFL players and more than 200 wins, now in his second year with his alma mater.
Fred Fusaro, 83, is in his second year as a volunteer offensive and defensive line coach at Huntington High School in Huntington, New York, his alma mater. The Blue Devils are 2-1 this season as Fusaro continues a coaching career spanning more than 55 years on Long Island. He is a former noseguard at Huntington and now works with the program he once played for as a varsity lineman in the 1960s.
Fusaro said the camaraderie he develops with young players is what keeps him coaching. He told The Post that if you get involved in coaching, you have to love it, and that he loves these kids. He described himself as a super senior in his second year with the Blue Devils. The team practices with Fusaro leading the offensive line, and photos from a Sept. 30, 2026 practice show him working in the huddle and running drills.
The coach spent 34 years as head coach at Sachem, a run that ended in 2002. He said he has more than 200 victories. Sachem North's varsity field now bears his name, honoring two Rutgers Cups, numerous county titles, and the character development he tried to instill in the young men of the Flaming Arrows over those three decades. Four of his athletes reached the NFL, most notably John (Jumbo) Elliott, a Giants Super Bowl champion.
Fusaro estimated that more than 150 of his players went on to college football over his 55 years of coaching. He called the number of former players who became coaches a minimum of 50 and said it makes him feel he did something right. Beyond wins and losses, he said the most humbling honor is seeing how many of his former players he inspired to become coaches.
Dave Shanahan, a former Sachem running back who helped lead the school to a 1986 Rutgers Trophy, said Fusaro is a humble man. Shanahan added that since he was a young man, Fusaro was always behind him and his decisions that Fusaro thought were good for him. Both acknowledged that the relationship was not always sunshine and rainbows, because some of the most impactful moments came through tough love that players took in stride.
After leaving Sachem, Fusaro was ready to stop dealing with parents but not with the kids. A full-circle opportunity came through Shanahan, who became head coach at John Glenn High School in Elwood in 1995. In 2004, Shanahan brought Fusaro on as an assistant. Fusaro said he figured he would be with Shanahan for a couple of years and ended up staying 19 years.
The pair won back-to-back Long Island championships in 2010 and 2011. Shanahan said Fusaro was instrumental in that success while running the Knights defense, adding that Fusaro had excellent schemes and is a true technician. Glenn's 2010 team had Long Island's only undefeated season and won a Rutgers Trophy.
Shanahan said the players loved Fusaro because he was such a hard worker, and Fusaro called Shanahan one of his best players. Fusaro said his approach made X's and O's a secondary objective to a bigger picture for teenagers, whether or not they were slated to play after high school. Shanahan added that by pushing players hard and holding them accountable, Fusaro prepared them not only for football but for the great game of life.
John Glenn boys soccer coach Lou Hanner overheard Shanahan talking about Fusaro and interjected to call him first class. Over the summer, Fusaro was inducted into the New York State Public High School Athletic Association Hall of Fame. He said he had 25 players come up to Buffalo for the induction, an entire first string of those he mentored standing with him for the honor.
When Shanahan retired from coaching in 2025, Fusaro said he knew it was time to go back to where it all began for him, the Blue Devils. Fusaro found his love for coaching from the staff he enjoyed as a varsity lineman in the 1960s, which led him to play for Ithaca and later coach at the college level with St. Lawrence and Hofstra. He said being back at Huntington brought back a lot of memories and that he has been truly blessed to have the kids and dedicated coaches he had over the years.
